title: Meritancing Scam or Legit? 2026 Review
description: Is Meritancing legit or a scam? We check its AI family-wealth claims, its Singapore address and the fee, regulator and pricing details its site leaves out.
author: James Whitmore
excerpt: Is Meritancing legit or a scam? We check its AI family-wealth claims, its Singapore address and the fee, regulator and pricing details its site leaves out.
content:
Meritancing describes itself as an AI-driven data analysis and risk management service for family wealth. Its site says it was built to act as a guardian for family savings, and that it was not built to trade on your behalf.

Searches for Meritancing usually ask whether it is legit or a scam. The site gives a Singapore address and a set of claims about its method, but it leaves out the details needed to check them, so this review sets out what it says and what is missing.

This review uses only what meritancing.net says about Meritancing. Claims the site makes without a source are attributed to it, and we say so where we could not check them.

Meritancing Explained: What the Site Describes

According to its site, Meritancing analyses market data in real time and says it adjusts a portfolio's risk posture automatically. It describes three life-stage options: education fund planning, retirement stability and generational wealth transfer.

The site describes a three-step method from data ingestion to a tailored recommendation. It says each recommendation can be traced back to its data, but it does not show an example.

Meritancing: Where the Site Stands Up, Where It Doesn’t

Here is what the site offers, and what it does not back up.

What Meritancing states about itself:

  • The site is clear that the service is for information and analysis rather than trading on your behalf.
  • A three-step method is described, and the site says recommendations come with their reasoning.
  • The site describes encryption of data in storage and in transit, and says data is not sold for marketing.
  • A Singapore address, a contact email and a phone number are shown, which gives you places to ask questions.

Where Meritancing Falls Short:

  • No fees, minimum amount, regulator or licence are stated, so the cost and legal status cannot be checked from the site.
  • The site says it was “not built to trade on your behalf” but also that it adjusts your portfolio's risk posture automatically. It does not explain who makes the change.
  • No example recommendation, track record or backtest is shown for the predictive model.
  • The phone number uses a US-format code, while the address is in Singapore. Confirm which office you are dealing with.
  • The company name and the people behind the model are not identified.

A confident description of a method is not proof that it works. Judge Meritancing on what you can verify.

What Happens Behind Meritancing, According to Its Site

The site says the model identifies recurring patterns across large datasets, including volatility cycles, sector behaviour and macroeconomic indicators, to anticipate shifts.

It says risk exposure is adjusted to match your stated goals and life stage, and that markets are monitored continuously, with allocation re-evaluated when conditions move outside expected ranges.

The site does not say how these predictions are tested, how often they are wrong, or what happens to your money when the model changes an allocation.

Getting Set Up: The Steps the Site Describes

This is the sign-up route as the Meritancing site lays it out. We did not open an account to check it.

1. Start the analysis

The site offers a “Start Analysis” button and says you share your goals and risk tolerance. It does not describe the form or what it asks.

2. Receive a recommendation

The site says you receive a clear, actionable insight with the reasoning behind it. It does not say whether recommendations come with a fee.

3. Decide

The site says the decision remains yours. It does not say how any money is invested, or who holds it.

We did not start the analysis. Ask in writing how your data is used, and whether any money is held or moved by Meritancing.

What Meritancing Costs: What the Site Says and Leaves Out

The site does not state a fee, subscription, minimum amount or performance charge. It mentions no pricing page.

Because the site does not say whether it charges for analysis, or takes a share of any investment result, the cost of using it is unknown.

Before you deposit, check these in writing:

  • Whether the analysis is free, a subscription, or charged per recommendation.
  • Any performance fee, and whether it is taken from your investment or paid separately.
  • Who holds your money, and what charges apply if money is invested through a third party.
  • Any cancellation or exit cost.

Ask for the full pricing in writing before you share any personal or financial data.

What Meritancing Offers

The site refers to global financial indicators, interest rates, currency movements and economic releases, and to a range of asset positions to adjust. It does not give a list of the assets it covers.

  • Global indicators and macroeconomic releases, described as inputs to the model.
  • Interest rates and currency movements, named as data sources.
  • Asset positions, described as adjustable, but not listed.

Ask which assets and products the recommendations can cover, and whether you would invest directly or through another provider.

Is Meritancing Legit?

The site says it was built around “measurable outcomes, not speculation”, and that recommendations are “built for clarity rather than speculation”. These are the site's own statements.

The site says it answers questions families ask before relying on an automated system, and it lists three questions about privacy, bias and whether the AI decides without you.

What we could and could not confirm from the site:

  • The legal entity behind Meritancing and its registration: not named.
  • Which regulator oversees it, and under which licence: not named.
  • Any measured outcome, track record or client result: not shown.
  • How the algorithm is tested for bias: asked as a question on the site, but the answer does not describe a test.

Checks you can run yourself:

  • Search the company name and address on the official register in Singapore, and the register of the country you live in.
  • Ask in writing for the legal entity name, its licence or exemption, and the name of the company that holds your money.
  • Ask for the model's track record, its testing method and the results of a live out-of-sample test.
  • Confirm the phone number and address match the company you are dealing with.
  • Search the name for independent reviews and complaints, and read them with care.

Advice on family wealth is generally regulated. Check that the service you use is authorised to provide it. This section is general information, not legal or financial advice.

Mistakes Worth Avoiding with Meritancing

Most losses on platforms like this come from the decisions people make after signing up. A few worth flagging:

Treating the description of the method as a track record.

The site shows no results. Ask for a verifiable record before you rely on it.

Sharing family financial data before you know the terms.

Read the privacy policy and ask in writing who sees your data.

Assuming an analysis tool is a regulated adviser.

Check the regulator and licence before you act on any recommendation.

Acting on one recommendation without a second opinion.

The site says decisions remain yours. Take advice from a licensed professional before a large move.

A Quick Checklist Before You Deposit

Run through this before you send any money.

  • The legal entity, licence and regulator found on the official register.
  • Full pricing, including any performance fee, obtained in writing.
  • The model's track record and testing method requested.
  • Your data-use and privacy terms read in full.
  • The company holding any money identified and checked.
  • A licensed adviser consulted before any large decision.

Who Meritancing May Suit, and Who Should Look Elsewhere

Meritancing may suit a family that wants an information-based analysis tool, will ask for the licence and pricing first, and treats any recommendation as one input among several.

It is a poor fit for anyone who needs a named regulator, a fee schedule or a sourced track record before sharing data or money.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Meritancing legit or a scam?

We could not confirm it. The site names no legal entity, regulator or licence, and it shows no track record.

Is Meritancing a scam?

We cannot say either way. Ask for the licence and pricing in writing, and check the Singapore address on the register.

Does Meritancing charge fees?

The site does not state any fee. Ask for the full pricing in writing.

What is the Meritancing minimum deposit?

The site does not state one, and it does not say whether you invest through the platform.

Does Meritancing trade on my behalf?

The site says it was not built to trade on your behalf, but also that it adjusts your portfolio's risk automatically. Ask who makes each change.

Where is Meritancing based?

The site lists 8 Jurong Town Hall Road, Singapore 609434. Confirm this on the company register.

Does Meritancing guarantee returns?

The site does not state a guarantee. It says the model anticipates shifts, but gives no track record. Investing carries a risk of loss.

Where We Land on Meritancing

The Meritancing site presents an AI analysis tool for family wealth, built to explain its reasoning. It does not name the company behind it, a regulator, a licence, a fee or a track record.

If you still want to look further, get the licence and pricing in writing, check the company on the register, and take licensed advice before you act on any recommendation.
